en: *Mahāyānalakṣaṇasamuccaya-śāstra*, Fascicle One.
Composed by Bodhisattva Jñānaśrīmitra.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master of the Western Heaven, Chao Feng Da Fu [and others].
Translated by the Imperial Preceptor and Dharma Master Shi Hu, recipient of the purple robe, by imperial decree. I take refuge in the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī.

I shall now briefly explain the characteristics of the various Mahāyāna teachings: arising from the bodhicitta and corresponding with great compassion, one should understand that all phenomena are indeed without self.
This is the characteristic of the knowable; therefore, it is explained now.
In this context, what is meant by "all phenomena" (*sarvadharma*)?

They are as follows: the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), the perfections (*pāramitā*), the stages (*bhūmi*), emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), the noble truths (*āryasatya*), the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), the formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*), the meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*), the preliminary practices (*prayoga*), the doors of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*), the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), the dhāraṇīs, the powers (*bala*), the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), great loving-kindness and great compassion (*mahāmaitrī-mahākaruṇā*), the unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*), the fruits of the śrāvakas, the thorough knowledge of all characteristics, suchness (*tathatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and the signless realm of phenomena (*animittadharmadhātu*). These are called "all phenomena."
What is called "aggregates" refers to the five aggregates. What are these five?
They are form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
In this context, "form" (*rūpa*) consists of the five sense faculties and the five objects.
The faculties refer to the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body.
The objects refer to visible form, sound, odor, taste, and tangible objects.

The basis of that visual consciousness is the pure eye-faculty; the basis of auditory consciousness is the pure ear-faculty; the basis of olfactory consciousness is the pure nose-faculty; the basis of gustatory consciousness is the pure tongue-faculty; and the basis of tactile consciousness is the pure body-faculty.
Form is of two kinds: color (varṇa) and shape (saṃsthāna).
Color refers to blue and so forth; shape refers to long and so forth.
Sound is of three kinds: that produced by appropriated primary elements, that produced by non-appropriated primary elements, and that produced by both.
There are two kinds of fragrance: namely, pleasant fragrance and unpleasant fragrance.
There are six kinds of taste: namely, bitter, sour, sweet, pungent, salty, and bland.
There are eleven kinds of tangibles, namely: solidity, moisture, warmth, motion, heaviness, lightness, smoothness, roughness, softness, hunger, and thirst.
To summarize these various contacts, there are three types: the agreeable, the disagreeable, and that which is intermediate between the two.

These, produced by the eye and so forth, when distinguished by way of realms, destinies, and the three periods of time, possess infinite subtle variations in their modes of activity; one should understand that such things are briefly described as the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
What is the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*)? There are three kinds of feeling: painful feeling, pleasant feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.

When these three feelings are distinguished according to the eye and so forth, they comprise six divisions; when further distinguished in that manner, there are eighteen types of feeling, as will be clearly explained in detail below in the section on the lower realm.

Regarding this aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*), if one were to distinguish it according to realms, destinies, and so forth, its modes of manifestation (*ākāra*) would be infinite; thus, these [points] should be understood as a brief explanation of the aggregate of sensation.
What is the aggregate of perception?
There are six kinds of perception.
Its mode of activity consists of six types, which are the discernment of the characteristics of their respective objects based on the eye and the other sense faculties.
The grasped characteristic refers to form (*rūpa*) and so forth; however, its underlying nature (*āśraya-svabhāva*) is indeed beyond conceptual differentiation.
Whether through conceptual differentiation or non-conceptual differentiation, it refers to the two dharmas of form (*rūpa*) and feeling (*vedanā*).
All such [phenomena] as these arise from their own respective categories within the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).

Regarding this aggregate of perception, if one were to analyze it according to realms (*dhātu*), destinies (*gati*), and so forth, its modes of activity (*ākāra*) would be boundless; one should know that all such things are briefly described here as the aggregate of perception.
What is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*)?

It refers to the mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), namely the categories of wholesome states such as faith and so forth, and the categories of afflictions (*kleśa*) such as greed, hatred, and delusion.
These mental factors, which serve as the bases for the various states of the mind, function in dependence upon the eye and other sense faculties.

Regarding this aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), if one were to differentiate it according to realms, destinies, and so forth, its modes of manifestation would be boundless; one should know that such things as these constitute a brief explanation of the aggregate of formations.
What is the aggregate of consciousness?
It refers to the six groups of consciousness.

As for this aggregate of consciousness, when distinguished according to the sense faculties such as the eye and their objects such as form, as well as by their specific characteristics and even by distinctions such as wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate, it possesses infinite modes of activity; one should know that such categories constitute a brief explanation of the aggregate of consciousness.
As previously stated in summary, these are called the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

As for what are called the bases (*āyatana*), they are the twelve bases: namely, the six internal bases—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—and the six external bases—form, sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, and mental phenomena (*dharma*).
In this context, it should be understood that the five faculties, such as the eye, and the five objects, such as form, constitute the ten bases of form (*rūpāyatana*).
That which is the mind-base (*manāyatana*) refers to the various consciousnesses;
all remaining phenomena constitute the base of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).
What is called the "elements" (dhātu) refers to the eighteen elements, namely: the six sense-faculty elements, the six object elements, and the six consciousness elements.
Within these, there are six distinct types of eye-consciousness and so forth; correspondingly, there are six types of contact, namely: eye-contact through to mind-contact.
Those consciousnesses of form and so forth possess three types of characteristics: namely, the wholesome, the unwholesome, and that which is intermediate between them.
This mode of activity serves as the causal nature for the arising of the three kinds of sensation through eye-contact and the other forms of contact.
Those three feelings arise from contact with the eye and so forth, making six; each of those six is further divided into three types, namely: painful, pleasant, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
Thus, it is said in general that there are eighteen types each of contact (*sparśa*) and feeling (*vedanā*).
As indicated previously regarding the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*), the same applies to their modes of activity (*ākāra*).
Furthermore, the characteristics of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness are called the six elements (*ṣaḍ-dhātu*).
Regarding what is called "dependent origination," what is its mode of operation?
It is precisely the twelvefold dependent origination. What are these twelve?
These refer to ignorance up to old age and death.

Herein, "ignorance" refers to incorrect engagement with respect to karma, its results, the truths, and the jewels. From this ignorance, various afflictions arise; therefore, within that which is selfless, one conceives of a self and perceives the aggregates and so forth as being substantially existent.

With ignorance as condition, there are volitional formations (saṃskāra). There are three kinds of volitional formations: meritorious formations, non-meritorious formations, and imperturbable formations.

Meritorious formations refer to the ten paths of wholesome action; non-meritorious formations refer to the ten paths of unwholesome action; and imperturbable formations refer to the formless attainments (ārūpya-samāpatti).
As he practices in this way, conditioned by ignorance, the various formations (saṃskāra) arise. With formations as a condition, consciousness arises;
thus, the seeds for the fruits of the agreeable and disagreeable—the various consciousnesses of the eye and so forth—grow and develop.
Consciousness conditions name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Regarding this "name-and-form," it is said that "name" is designated by virtue of consciousness, as name has its place of arising therein.
Therefore, the four aggregates beginning with feeling (*vedanā*) constitute "name," while "form" is established in dependence upon name as appropriate.
With name-and-form as condition, there are the six sense bases. As for those six sense bases, they are established by means of such name-and-form as the six bases beginning with the eye.
With the six sense bases as condition, there is contact; "contact" refers to the eyes and so forth, and forms and so forth, as has already been explained previously.

Conditioned by contact (sparśa) arises feeling (vedanā); there are three kinds of feeling, as previously explained. Herein, contact and feeling should be understood as associated with formations (saṃskāra).
Conditioned by feeling arises craving (tṛṣṇā); craving arises from ignorance (avidyā).
Craving conditions grasping; grasping refers to the pleasurable engagement arising from that which is grasped, such as form and so forth.
Grasping conditions becoming; the characteristic of becoming refers to the characteristics of volitional formations, consciousness, and so forth, exactly as previously described.

There is birth conditioned by [ignorance], meaning that name-and-form arises; because of that ignorance, there is the phenomenon of birth, and the intrinsic nature of this ignorance itself has no distinct stages.
Birth conditions old age and death: "old age" refers to the decay and transformation of the aggregates (*skandhas*), and "death" refers to the dissolution and disintegration of the aggregates.
At the final limit of the phenomena of birth, there is no substantial reality; one completely abandons the body previously acquired.

Nevertheless, that ignorance continues to function within the subsequent aggregates, increasing all afflictions and faults; since these are all caused by ignorance itself and its own kind—namely, afflictions and karma—afflictions, karma, and birth arise.
These three are not severed, and by means of them, saṃsāra continues in its successive flow.
One who understands this should give rise to the antidote toward actual phenomena, realizing that the intrinsic nature of ignorance and the other [afflictions] is selfless.
Thus, the dependent origination of twelve links has been briefly explained.
As for what are called the *pāramitās*, what are their characteristics?
Their number is ten.
In this context, there are three kinds of giving: namely, the gift of Dharma, the gift of non-deception, and the gift of loving-kindness.
There are three kinds of ethical discipline: namely, the discipline of restraint, the discipline of gathering virtuous dharmas, and the discipline of benefiting sentient beings.

There are three types of patience (*kṣānti*): namely, patience through the discernment of phenomena (*dharmanidhyānakṣānti*), patience in enduring enmity and harm (*paropakramakṣānti*), and patience in accepting suffering (*duḥkhādhivāsanakṣānti*).

There are three types of diligence (*vīrya*): namely, the diligence of donning armor (*saṃnāhavīrya*), the diligence of application (*prayogavīrya*), and the diligence of ultimate accomplishment (*niṣṭhāgamana-vīrya*).
There are three kinds of concentration: namely, concentration that eliminates faults, concentration that brings about realization, and concentration that accomplishes tasks.
There are three kinds of wisdom: namely, wisdom derived from hearing, wisdom derived from reflection, and wisdom derived from cultivation.
There are three kinds of skillful means (*upāya*): namely, the skillful means of avoiding faults, the skillful means of providing relief, and the skillful means of swiftly attaining bliss.

There are three kinds of vows (*praṇidhāna*): namely, the vow for the accomplishment of one’s own practice, the vow to liberate sentient beings from their bonds, and the vow to purify the Buddha-field.
There are three kinds of power: the power to accomplish tasks, the power to eliminate afflictions, and the power to subdue Māra and his enemies.
There are three kinds of wisdom: non-conceptual wisdom, the wisdom that discerns and realizes equality, and the wisdom that extinguishes the sins of sentient beings.
Thus, these perfections such as generosity are preceded by the bodhicitta, and one should cultivate the contemplation of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings.
Yet, regarding the practice of these perfections within the world, there is neither a mode of activity nor anything to be apprehended;
regarding the supramundane aggregates and so forth, they are the very mark of selflessness and liberation, which is to be contemplated according to reality as it is truly realized.

As for what are called the "grounds," they are the ten grounds, namely: the Ground of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), where one cultivates the perfection of generosity (*dāna-pāramitā*); the Ground of Purity (*vimalā-bhūmi*), where one cultivates the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*); the Ground of Radiance (*prabhākārī-bhūmi*), where one cultivates the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*); the Ground of Blazing Wisdom (*arciṣmatī-bhūmi*), where one cultivates the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*); the Ground Difficult to Conquer (*sudurjayā-bhūmi*), where one cultivates the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*); the Ground of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), where one cultivates the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*); the Ground of Far-Going (*dūraṃgamā-bhūmi*), where one cultivates the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*); the Ground of Immovability (*acalā-bhūmi*), where one cultivates the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*); the Ground of Good Intelligence (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*), where one cultivates the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*); and the Ground of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), where one cultivates the perfection of gnosis (*jñāna-pāramitā*).
Thus, the principle of the selflessness of phenomena attained across all these stages is realized through the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and is entirely without distinction.

Nevertheless, the various *pāramitās* such as generosity (*dāna*) that he cultivates are established upon the attainment of pure and supreme excellence; they are universally accomplished through the power of vast vows and are not shared with any of the śrāvakas or others.
These pāramitās are without differentiation regarding their objective referents—whether persons or phenomena—because they are devoid of signs and empty.
That which is called "emptiness" refers to the eighteen kinds of emptiness; that is to say, the emptiness of the eye and so forth is termed "internal emptiness."
Form and so forth are empty; this is called "emptiness of the external.
When wisdom contemplates the equality of the eye and so forth with form and so forth, it is called "emptiness of the internal and external.
When one observes each of the various parts of the directions and the characteristics of the receptacle world, finding that each and every one is empty, this is called "great emptiness."

The nature of being free from grasping and rejecting within all conceptual constructions is called emptiness; that this emptiness is itself empty is called the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*).
That which cannot be apprehended when observing the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is called the emptiness of the ultimate (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
The fact that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*), such as the practice of giving and so forth, are entirely equal is called the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtaśūnyatā*).
The fact that all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma*) lack the characteristic of being awakened to or produced is called the emptiness of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛtaśūnyatā*).

Within the dharma of emptiness, there is not the slightest dharma that can truly be transformed or dispersed such that it ceases to accumulate; this is called the emptiness of dispersion (*vibhava-śūnyatā*).
All those dharmas are without limit or boundary; this is called the emptiness of the limitless (*anavara-agra-śūnyatā*).
Among all phenomena (*dharma*), there is ultimately not even a single phenomenon that is not empty; this is called "ultimate emptiness" (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).

The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the aggregates (*skandha*) and other phenomena is likewise such: they are without arising and are free from the characteristics of self-grasping and rejection; this is called "emptiness of specific characteristics" (*svalakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).
The emptiness of all phenomena without distinction is called the "emptiness of all phenomena.
The fact that within my aggregates neither grasping nor abandoning can be apprehended is called the "emptiness of the unapprehendable."
This is unobtainable because the characteristics of form and so forth are unobtainable; there exists only the nature of karma, which is called the emptiness of signlessness (*animitta-śūnyatā*).
Whether it be persons or phenomena, their intrinsic nature is empty; this is called the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*).
Among all natures, that which is free from the nature of grasping and abandoning is called the emptiness of non-nature (*abhāva-śūnyatā*).
That "non-nature" refers to the fact that there is no distinct nature apart from the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth.

If one were to give rise to conceptual discrimination regarding emptiness with respect to the intrinsic nature of the aggregates and so forth, this would be a characteristic of obstruction; it is then called the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-nature (*abhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*).

If one reaches the point where such conceptualization is exhausted, one is able to be liberated from the fetters of form and so forth; no longer conceptualizing the existence or non-existence of boundaries, and being free from the grasping and abandoning of the aggregates and so on—this is the single characteristic.
Yet that single characteristic is non-dual; because it is thus, one abides in a single-pointed focus upon the *pāramitās*.
The principle of intrinsic emptiness, free from the marks of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), is the true object of observation regarding selflessness.
What are called the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa) are the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, namely, the four foundations of mindfulness up to the eightfold noble path.
The four foundations of mindfulness are: body, feeling, mind, and phenomena.

Among these, the foundation of mindfulness of the body consists of contemplating that the body has no various accumulations and is without attachment; being free from the characteristics of grasping and rejecting, this is called the foundation of mindfulness of the body.
One should likewise contemplate the foundations of mindfulness of feeling, mind, and phenomena.

Furthermore, within this very foundation of mindfulness of phenomena, if one distinguishes between the internal, external, and intermediate, there are three distinct types: namely, diligence, concentration, and right mindfulness.
This threefold association enables one to contemplate the most supreme bodhicitta of all bodhisattvas as well as their virtuous practices such as generosity.
Among all phenomena, attaining association with selflessness is the most supreme of these reflections.
Thus, these are briefly called the four foundations of mindfulness; one should know that all other dharmas are likewise.
As for the four right efforts, they refer to the factors to be counteracted and are not themselves factors of enlightenment.

To cause what has already arisen to be abandoned and what has not yet arisen not to arise—this is called the diligent abandonment of the two types of unwholesome states; these are not the factors to be counteracted, but rather the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa*).
To cause what has not yet arisen to arise and what has already arisen to increase—this is called the diligent cultivation of the two types of wholesome states.
Thus, in brief, these are called the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).
As for the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), they consist of desire, diligence, concentration, and wisdom.

The fruits obtained through the predominance of such corresponding practices are the objects of observation—namely, desire and so forth—by means of what has been attained; these are the four kinds of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Furthermore, when that body and mind are detached from all bases, dwelling in the thought of freedom from craving, and relying upon the cessation of all conditioned activities—
this, briefly stated, is called the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*).

The five faculties and five powers refer to the thorough understanding of all marks and fruits; that is, the faculties and powers associated with the predominance of faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
Thus, in brief, these are called the five faculties (pañcendriya) and the five powers (pañcabala).
Furthermore, the practices cultivated therein consist of two factors of enlightenment (bodhyaṅga), namely the stages of Heat (ūṣmagata) and Summits (mūrdhan).
At the stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*), one cultivates the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*); at the stage of Summits (*mūrdhan*), one cultivates the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*).
Furthermore, there are two superior factors of clear comprehension (*abhisamaya-aṅga*), namely: Patience (*kṣānti*) and the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*).

In the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), one cultivates the four bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*); in the stage of the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), one cultivates the five faculties (*indriya*) and the five powers (*bala*).
Such practices as these are the unconditioned activity, the most supreme reality.

The faculties and powers, such as faith and the rest, serve as the causal conditions for the aspect of the path of seeing; it should be understood that what is cultivated during that path of seeing is called the seven factors of enlightenment.
These seven factors of enlightenment are, namely, the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness up to the factor of enlightenment of equanimity.

Among these, the awakening factor of mindfulness is characterized by the presence of right mindfulness without forgetfulness, consisting of the vow to benefit sentient beings and realize enlightenment.
The awakening factor of investigation of phenomena is characterized by the discernment of the intrinsic nature of self and phenomena.

The factor of enlightenment of joy (*prīti-saṃbodhyaṅga*) refers to the arising of joy and bliss born from the cause of attaining the untainted (*anāsrava*) state through the path cultivated by oneself.

The factor of enlightenment of pliancy (*praśrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*) refers to the attainment of physical and mental pliancy by abandoning that which is not the seed of the factors of enlightenment, in accordance with the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as it has been realized.

The awakening factor of concentration refers to the four immeasurables and the state of a single-pointed object of focus consisting of the wisdom that enters into suchness, accompanied by the vow for enlightenment.

The awakening factor of diligence refers to not becoming attached to the gates of the sublime qualities of tranquility while observing them, and proceeding to cultivate all practices without slackening or ceasing.

The factor of awakening of equanimity refers to being mindful of benefiting sentient beings according to how they should be disciplined, and—following their respective practices of the *pāramitās* and other meritorious qualities—equally discerning that these have neither coming nor going, because one abides in equanimity.
Thus, in brief, these are called the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).

These very factors of the seven limbs of enlightenment are termed the "portion of right knowledge" (*samyagjñānabhāga*), as they serve as the antidote to the modes of activity of both the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
It should be understood that what is cultivated in the path of cultivation is precisely the Eightfold Noble Path.
The Eightfold Noble Path consists of right view through to right concentration.
Among these, right view refers to the thorough realization that all phenomena lack the characteristic of self, abiding in equanimity.
The inversions such as suffering and so forth—those two aspects—are the subtle characteristics observed by superior wisdom (*viśeṣajñāna*).
"Right reflection" (*samyak-saṃkalpa*) refers to the arising of reflection that does not sever the causes of what is to be done, thereby realizing the fruit according to one's aspiration.
Right speech refers to all forms of verbal expression that are free from false conceptualization and are spoken in accordance with reality.
Right action refers to all deeds performed without inversion—such as not harming sentient beings and rescuing them—which are practiced while remaining free from delusion.
Right Livelihood means that regarding a pure livelihood, one is free from all forms of deviance and falsehood, practicing what one has cultivated and realizing it through one's own practice.
Right Effort means that even upon reaching the highest stages, one continues to progress further, with no physical fatigue and a mind characterized by courageous vigor.

Right mindfulness means observing the foundations of mindfulness and so forth as they truly are; adorned with a compassionate mind and the skillful means of one’s own vows, one does not forget or lose any phenomenon.

Right concentration refers to bodily and other actions that constantly rely upon supreme merit and abide in non-conceptual wisdom; it is the state of being in equal correspondence with the characteristics of all meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*).

These and others, briefly explained, are called the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), because they collectively and concisely encompass the modes of practice as appropriate.

Furthermore, that which is called the Noble Truths refers to the Four Noble Truths: namely, suffering, origination, cessation, and the path.
Among these, the Noble Truth of Suffering refers to the inverted characteristics of the aggregates and so forth, having as its nature that which is contrary to the noble Dharma.

The Noble Truth of Origination refers to the aforementioned suffering, which—conditioned by the accumulation of afflictions and karma such as ignorance (*avidyā*) and volitional formations (*saṃskāra*)—serves as the causal nature for the suffering of birth and so forth.

The noble truth of cessation refers to that which has the nature of non-conceptualization and the characteristic of non-arising regarding all phenomena as they truly are; it is the cessation realized as the antidote to the darkness of worldly ignorance.
The Noble Truth of the Path refers to the dharmas such as the mind of loving-kindness directed toward awakening and the application of mindfulness to dharmas, because it subsumes them all in brief.
These noble truths take all dharmas as their object with impartiality.

Thus, in brief, these are called the Four Noble Truths. As for what is termed "meditative concentration" (dhyāna), it refers to the four meditative concentrations: that which is characterized by joy and bliss born of seclusion is called the first dhyāna; that which is characterized by joy and bliss born of concentration is called the second dhyāna; that which is characterized by sublime bliss free from joy is called the third dhyāna; and that which is characterized by purity of equanimity and mindfulness is called the fourth dhyāna.
These four are all characterized by quiescence; because the mind of desire and so forth does not fluctuate within the realms of existence, they are called *dhyāna*.

Nevertheless, the bodhisattvas do not relish or become attached to the bliss of these meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), for they never abandon sentient beings, perfecting the dharmas of the bodhisattva path and accomplishing immeasurable practices.
Thus, in brief, these are called the four dhyānas.

As for what are termed the "immeasurable practices," they are the four immeasurable practices—namely, loving-kindness (maitrī), compassion (karuṇā), sympathetic joy (muditā), and equanimity (upekṣā)—for all four take immeasurable sentient beings as their objective sphere.

Regarding the practice of immeasurable loving-kindness herein: it consists of bestowing ultimate benefit and happiness upon all sentient beings; all practices thus cultivated are entirely free from signs (*nimitta*), remain far removed from inversion (*viparyāsa*), and accord with the Bodhisattva path.
The practice of immeasurable compassion (*karuṇā*) means not allowing a single sentient being to experience suffering.
This compassion has as its nature the non-arising of affliction and harm, serving as the antidote to them.

The practice of immeasurable sympathetic joy (*muditā*) means realizing the equality of selflessness in all phenomena; it consists of the joyful feeling that arises from the skillful means of practicing generosity and other virtues while abiding in the bodhicitta for the sake of extensively benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings.

To relinquish immeasurable practices means to regard the three realms of existence with equanimity, to initiate vast conduct for the sake of rescuing sentient beings, and not to relish or become attached to the bliss of the samādhis one has attained.
This serves as the antidote to the fault of negligence; with the mind abiding in the true nature of reality (*dharmatā*), one appropriately subdues all worldly minds that cling to signs (*nimitta*).

Having already attained stability in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one applies the antidote of the true dharma to all perceptions of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*) and further attains equality regarding the infinite gateways of the Dharma. Thus abiding in the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), one realizes it in accordance with reason.
All the dharmas of equal bliss thus obtained are called the most excellent attainment of mastery.
This brief explanation is termed the practice of the four immeasurables (*catur-apramāṇa*).

As for what is called the formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*), there are four of them, namely: the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

Regarding the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) of the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) among these: it refers to being free from various perceptions of form and resistance, contemplating infinite space as the corresponding object, relinquishing all signs of existence, and abiding with the mind focused on a single point.

Furthermore, the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) of the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—all such states are practices of tranquility. Just as in the initial application one takes the characteristic of non-attachment as the object of observation, one further contemplates non-clinging and non-obstruction, whereby the supreme signless (*animitta*) arises accordingly.
Thus, in brief, these are called the four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*).

As for what are called "liberations" (*vimokṣa*), they refer to the eight liberations, namely: the liberation of one who possesses internal perception of forms while observing external forms, up to and including the liberation of the cessation of sensation and perception (*saṃjñā-vedayita-nirodha-vimokṣa*).

Among these, the first liberation refers to having the perception of internal forms while being free from craving for external forms; this is called the liberation of perceiving external forms with internal form.

Furthermore, according to its specific mode of practice, it refers to being without the perception of internal forms while being free from craving for external forms; this is called the liberation of perceiving external forms without internal form.
Furthermore, dwelling in the purity of form and so forth with a practice free from greed is called the liberation of purity (*śubha-vimokṣa*).

Furthermore, the liberation of the sphere of infinite space, the liberation of the sphere of infinite consciousness, the liberation of the sphere of nothingness, and the liberation of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—these four liberations of the formless spheres all abide in accordance with their respective modes of activity through observation as it truly is.

Furthermore, regarding the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of the liberation through the cessation of sensation and perception (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha-vimokṣa*), it should be understood that this brief explanation is termed the "eight liberations.

As for what is called the "preliminary practice" (*pūrvagamana*) of the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*): this refers to when one wishes to abide in those various meditative attainments such as the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*), one must first, as appropriate, extinguish all modes of activity and abide in the equality and tranquility of the intrinsic nature of phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*). Only thereafter should one settle into the various meditative attainments; this is termed the "preliminary practice."

Furthermore, it should be known that regarding these four formless attainments (*ārūpya-samāpatti*) and the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), Bodhisattvas enter the Lion’s Play Samādhi (*siṃhavikrīḍita-samādhi*) while they are present before them; they do not allow themselves to be interrupted by a mind that is not in meditative equipoise (*asamāhita-citta*), nor do they allow themselves to be interrupted by the first dhyāna or other such states.
This attainment of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti) is characterized by immovability.
Regarding the various meditative absorptions (samāpatti) herein, why is their sequence as it is?
It is because the sequence is such that it accords with the manner in which sentient beings are to be matured through observation.

Furthermore, one should know that this is the gateway to the supreme bliss. Those who attain this bliss realize that the self has no reality; because the self has no reality, one's own mind becomes tranquil.
All the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), perfections (*pāramitā*), and so forth that ought to be cultivated, arise as they truly are through the observation of supreme wisdom (*prajñā*).
This briefly summarizes the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).

As for what are called the "gateways to liberation" (*vimokṣamukha*), they are the three gateways to liberation, namely: emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).

Regarding the emptiness liberation door herein: it refers to the fact that whether persons or phenomena, such as the aggregates and so forth, are devoid of conceptual characteristics; and that these aggregates, whether defiled or purified, ultimately lack intrinsic nature within the sphere of conceptual characteristics. Within the dharma of emptiness, one is free from the characteristics of grasping or abandoning, and non-defiled wisdom correctly applies its antidote in accordance with reality.

The gate of liberation of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*) refers to the ultimate signlessness of the aggregates and so forth; because they are signless, they cannot be apprehended, and thus that non-defiled wisdom correctly counteracts them by not clinging to any signs.

The door of liberation of wishlessness refers to knowing, as they truly are, all aspects of the pure doors of liberation, the aggregates, bases, and elements, as well as the supreme practices for the perfection of the *pāramitās*; it arises from suchness and manifests in equanimity, because the mind is free from the aspiration and attachment that grasp at objects.
Thus, in brief, these are called the three gates of liberation.

As for what are termed supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), there are six kinds, namely, from the supernormal power of the divine eye up to the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*).
Among these, the supernormal power of the divine eye refers to the supreme purity that correctly perceives all forms and appearances without obstruction.
The supernormal power of the divine ear refers to the purity that is able to hear all sounds.
The supernormal power of knowing others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) refers to the ability to know all aspects of another's mind exactly as they are.
The supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti*) refers to the ability to remember all the various distinct events of one's own and others' past.

Regarding the supernormal power of the divine realm (*ṛddhividhi-abhijñā*), there are three aspects: mastery over concealment and manifestation; appearing in various forms throughout all worlds at will; and moving through the void without obstruction.
He manifests his body according to what is required for those he encounters, and performs miraculous feats by either manifesting or not manifesting bodily forms as appropriate.

Regarding the supernormal power of the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-abhijñā*): "outflows" refers to the afflictions such as ignorance and craving; their complete eradication through wisdom, leaving nothing remaining, is called the destruction of the outflows.

Such supreme sixfold superknowledges, which abide in the bodhicitta and possess wisdom free from conceptual proliferation, are the preeminent practices cultivated by these Bodhisattvas, not shared with the paths of the Śrāvakas and others.
The perfection of signlessness and non-awakening is the practice of the equal path of all *pāramitās*.
It comprehensively encompasses all white dharmas to be cultivated, by virtue of all aspirational powers and all characteristics.
With courageous diligence as the precursor, one abides in the supreme, pure one-pointedness of mind.

This is because the various distinctions corresponding to the names and meanings of the first dhyāna and so forth are subsumed within their infinite aspects, and because they are sustained by samādhi.
Thus, in brief, these are called the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).

As for what is termed *dhāraṇī*, it refers to the comprehensive inclusion, as appropriate, of all marks (*sarvanimitta*), all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), and the intrinsic nature of all phenomena (*sarvadharmatā*).
Names, phrases, and syllables constitute the characteristics of all meanings.

All immeasurable mindfulness, boundless eloquence, and various gateways of samādhi can be fully realized through this signless wisdom; because it counteracts the mind that possesses signs and obstructions, this is the supreme gateway of dhāraṇī attained in unsurpassed bodhi.

Furthermore, all those samādhis, dhāraṇīs, and so forth, are realized through the manifestation of the vajropama-samādhi; thus, with all characteristics universally equal, one enters and realizes the reality of signless wisdom.

Having completely relinquished all habitual tendencies, one observes with wisdom in equanimity and accords with great compassion; firm in one's actions, one attains liberation in accordance with reality regarding the nature of all phenomena. With superior retribution manifesting before one, one dwells in equanimity, and the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom arises in accordance with reality, whereby all powers of aspiration are fully perfected.
This brief explanation is called *dhāraṇī*.

As for what is called "power," it refers to the ten powers of a Buddha, namely, the power of knowing what is possible and impossible, up to the power of knowing the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-jñānabala*).

Among these, the power of knowledge regarding what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*) refers to knowing, as it truly is, the certainty and uncertainty of cause and effect in all circumstances.
Whether it be a Buddha, a Brahmā King, or a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin*), the fact that the superior rewards they obtain are certain is termed "the possible" (*sthāna*).
That which is "not possible" (asthāna) should be understood as the non-determinacy of cause and effect in their application.

As for the power of knowledge regarding the results of karma (*karmavipākajñānabala*), it refers to the knowledge that knows, in accordance with reality, how sentient beings perform wholesome or unwholesome deeds and are reborn in happy or miserable realms, as well as the specific results of such karmic actions.
The power of knowledge regarding the various elements (*nānādhātu-jñānabala*) refers to knowing, as they truly are, the distinctions among the realms and destinies of all sentient beings.

The power of knowledge regarding various inclinations (*nānādhimukti-jñānabala*) refers to knowing, as they truly are, how śrāvakas and others give rise to various inclinations toward phenomena—such as turning away from defiled states and proceeding toward the state of tranquility—and so forth.

The power of knowing the diversity of the faculties (*indriya*) means that one knows, according to reality, the various distinctions among the faculties of sentient beings, such as faith and the rest.

The power of knowing the diversity of meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) means that one knows, according to reality, the various *samādhis* and *samāpattis*, such as the first dhyāna and so forth, in all their infinite aspects, both according to their names and their meanings.
Regarding the power of knowledge concerning the path leading to the various destinations, there are two kinds of paths: the unwholesome path, which consists of ignorance and so forth;
and the wholesome path, which consists of cessation and so forth.
As for that cessation, it refers to the distinctions realized by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, which he knows with wisdom as they truly are.
Regarding the power of knowledge of birth and cessation, it means that he knows with wisdom, as they truly are, the various births and cessations of all sentient beings.
The power of knowledge consisting of the recollection of past abodes refers to the accurate recollection of past events as they truly were.

The power of knowledge consisting of the destruction of the outflows refers to the Buddha, the World-Honored One, observing through the nature of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, which is free from all obstructions, defilements, and conceptual discrimination, and is characterized by equality.
Such powers as the knowledge of what is possible and what is impossible are realized through the Tathāgata’s playful superknowledges.
Because he is fully endowed with these powers, all phenomena are the object of his supreme contemplation.
Thus, these are briefly explained as the ten powers (*daśabala*).

As for what is called fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*), it refers to the four grounds of self-confidence: namely, fearlessness regarding all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā-vaiśāradya*), fearlessness regarding the destruction of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-vaiśāradya*), fearlessness regarding the teaching on obstacles to the path (*antarāyika-dharma-deśanā-vaiśāradya*), and fearlessness regarding the teaching on the path leading out of suffering (*nairyāṇika-mārga-deśanā-vaiśāradya*).
Regarding such matters as whether these are different or not different, whatever may be spoken of, all are unfindable; thus one attains fearlessness and mastery.

These four are all observed through the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*), which is universally impartial according to the inclinations of sentient beings, like a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*).
This Dharma is likewise: the mark of self is pure and free from all attachments.
Thus, in brief, are the four fearlessnesses explained.
As for what is called "unimpeded understanding," it refers to the unimpededness regarding meaning (*artha*), phenomena (*dharma*), eloquence (*pratibhāna*), and analytical skill (*nirukti*).
Among these, the analytical knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*) refers to observing all sentient beings with the mark of selflessness through subtle wisdom in a state of equality.
The analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*) refers to the wisdom that understands all phenomena according to their respective characteristics, observing them as equal.

The analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*) means that according to what one wishes to speak, both the speaker and the spoken do not deviate from their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

The analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*) means that regarding boundless gateways of the Dharma, one penetrates them through appropriate discrimination as being signless (*animitta*).

All such [teachings] as these are associated with the sovereignty over all phenomena; they are intended to gather in those who are deluded, so that they may all be tamed and established in the equality of all phenomena, which is free from signs.
These four are all observed by means of the wisdom of wondrous discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*).
Thus, the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) have been briefly explained.

As for what is called "great loving-kindness" (*maitrī*) and "great compassion" (*karuṇā*): herein, loving-kindness refers to bestowing happiness upon sentient beings; it abides in a mind of tranquility, free from the characteristics of conceptual arousal, vast, most excellent, signless, and impartial.
Compassion means uprooting suffering, subduing that which is difficult to subdue, not abandoning sentient beings, and being free from all marks of existence.
Both of these are observed by the wisdom of accomplished action (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).
Thus has great loving-kindness and great compassion been briefly explained.

As for what are called the Buddha’s unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), they are the eighteen unique qualities, namely: the Tathāgata’s body is without fault, up to his present knowledge and vision being unattached and unimpeded.
Among these, the first refers to the Tathāgata’s body being without fault, free from weariness, and devoid of all physical defects.
The Tathāgata’s speech being without fault means that there is no unloving speech, and it is free from all verbal defects.
That the Tathāgata’s mind is without error means that he is free from lapses of mindfulness and has abandoned all faults of the mind.
These three types of action [of body, speech, and mind] are intended to inspire pure faith in those who are ignorant.
One who has no mind of divergent thoughts dwells with a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings.
One who has no unsettled mind acts to cause ignorant sentient beings to eliminate the signs of distraction.
There is no one who does not possess the mind of relinquishment; that is to say, there are no matters concerning sentient beings that one knows and yet relinquishes.
These six dharmas arise from the training in higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*) and serve as the cause for non-abiding nirvāṇa (*apratisthita-nirvāṇa*).
"Faith without diminution" means that faith is unimpaired within non-abiding nirvana.
"Aspiration without diminution" means that there is no attachment or craving toward non-abiding nirvana.
Vigour that does not diminish means that one dwells nowhere regarding gain, life, or conduct.
Wisdom that does not diminish means that one ultimately attains thorough penetration into all ways of nurturing sentient beings within the world.
"Non-diminution of liberation" means not grasping at the marks of the nirvana of the śrāvakas and others.

"Non-diminution of the knowledge and vision of liberation" means that, for the benefit of sentient beings, wisdom destroys the marks of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), causing all sentient beings to each equally realize unsurpassed nirvana.
These six dharmas arise from that training in higher concentration (*adhi-samādhi-śikṣā*) and serve as the conditions for non-abiding nirvāṇa (*apratiṣṭhita-nirvāṇa*).

Regarding "physical action follows wisdom": this means that in all circumstances—whether moving or stationary, walking, or standing—the various modes of conduct are always in constant association with wisdom; therefore, wisdom acts as the precursor.

Regarding "verbal action follows the movement of wisdom": this means that all speech is free from false discrimination and is constantly in accord with wisdom; therefore, wisdom serves as its precursor.

Regarding "mental action that follows wisdom": this refers to abiding in a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings, acting for their benefit without distinction, and being constantly in accord with wisdom; therefore, wisdom serves as the precursor.

Regarding "unattached and unimpeded knowledge and vision of the past": being without intrinsic nature internally is called "unattached," and being free from all external bonds is called "unimpeded. Thus, one knows all dharmas of the past with equanimity, destroying the characteristics of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

"Unattached and unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding the future" means that one knows all phenomena of the future with equanimity and completely destroys the marks of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
"Unattached and unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding the present" means that one knows all phenomena of the present with equanimity and completely destroys the marks of conceptual proliferation.
These six dharmas arise from that training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*).

These various dharmas are exclusively those perfectly accomplished by the Buddha-Tathāgata through his unsurpassed, supreme knowledge; they function in accordance with sentient beings for their benefit and are not shared with any of the śrāvakas, as they arise from the pure wisdom of the *dharmadhātu*.
Thus, in brief, these are called the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).
As for what is termed the fruit of the śrāvaka, it refers to the four fruits of the śrāvaka, namely from srotāpanna up to arhat.

Among these, the *srotāpanna* (stream-enterer) is one who, weary of suffering and aspiring toward bliss, eliminates all afflictions as appropriate; having seen the truths such as suffering through seven rounds of birth and death, they realize the selflessness of persons and proceed toward *nirvāṇa*.

The Sakṛdāgāmin (Once-returner) is one who, weary of suffering and rejoicing in bliss, eliminates all afflictions as appropriate; returning once more to this realm, they perceive the truths such as suffering, realize the selflessness of persons, and proceed toward Nirvāṇa.

The Anāgāmin, weary of suffering and rejoicing in bliss, has no further afflictions of the desire realm to be abandoned; thus, he does not return to the desire realm. Within the form and formless realms, he attains liberation as appropriate through the vision of the truths such as suffering, realizes the non-existence of a person (*pudgalanairātmya*), and proceeds toward *nirvāṇa*.

An Arhat has completely severed all afflictions within the three realms, reached the ultimate limit of suffering, realized the principle of non-self, and accordingly attained liberation, proceeding toward the realization of Nirvana.
Thus, the four fruits of the śrāvaka have been briefly explained.
As for the phrase "thoroughly knowing all characteristics," it means that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, thoroughly know all characteristics as they truly are, manifesting them with equanimity.
All characteristics are, in fact, all phenomena.
For the benefit of the world, the Buddhas and Tathāgatas employ all appropriate skillful means according to circumstances; they attain the state of non-delusion and abide in the mark of firmness.
In this context, it should be understood that the three bodies are also called "all aspects.
The Dharma-body is the aspect of the wisdom of selflessness by nature, because it is without differentiation.
The Enjoyment-body is the supreme aspect, because it is the very nature upon which all-aspect wisdom relies.
The emanation body (nirmāṇakāya) is so called because it manifests and establishes various activities and characteristics in all places as appropriate.

Furthermore, regarding all these characteristics, although they are fully understood, there is no conceptual discrimination; rather, one performs whatever actions are necessary in accordance with the needs of sentient beings for their benefit.
This characteristic is quiescent; being without objective conditions, its intrinsic nature is entirely equal.

All characteristics of the aggregates and so forth are likewise boundless. Whether within the three realms or beyond the three realms, one should understand, in accordance with reality, that all characteristics are unattainable.
This is called the thorough knowledge of all characteristics.

That which is termed "suchness" (tathatā) is the very nature of all phenomena, free from grasping or rejecting; whether wisdom or ignorance, whether form or mind, it abides in the state of equality, is free from delusion, and is non-conceptual—this is what is named suchness.
That which is called the "limit of reality" (bhūtakoṭi) is the very nature of bodhi; it is, in all its measure and according to reality, free from all conceptual discrimination.

In this regard, one should understand that as the Buddha has taught, the nature of the self, the aggregates, and so forth is ultimately unapprehendable, and furthermore, it cannot be expressed by any other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
This is what is called the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
That which is called "signless" (*animitta*) is precisely that suchness (*tathatā*) designated as signless.
As for suchness, it is merely a provisional conceptualization by means of names; therefore, within names, no intrinsic nature can be found.

One should know that our own nature is the self-nature of all phenomena; therefore, within this state, both persons and phenomena are entirely free from all characteristics and share a single characteristic.

This single characteristic is the non-obstructive characteristic of all phenomena, which is free from all conceptual discrimination and remains unmoving within the self-nature of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
This is called the signless (*animitta*).

That which is called the "dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu*) refers to the resultant dharmas such as the ten powers (*daśabala*), as well as all causal dharmas, up to the basis for the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all dharmas; this is the dharma-realm.
Within this dharma-realm, all false, inverted, and conceptualized characteristics are far removed; clear wisdom manifests and illuminates reality as it truly is.
This is called the dharma-realm.
Furthermore, it should be known that herein, suchness and so forth, as well as the great perfect mirror wisdom and so forth, are the gateways of non-action for all phenomena.
That gateway of non-action of suchness is itself the gateway of the intrinsic characteristics of all phenomena.
Furthermore, it should be known that herein, both suchness and those ten powers are all observed by means of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).
That which is realized as the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*) are all observed by means of the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*).

That signless, subtle, and pure nature, as well as the nature of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), are all observed by means of the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*).

That nature which is the basis for the realization of the reality of all phenomena within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), as well as great loving-kindness and great compassion, are all observed by means of the wisdom of accomplished action (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*).
All phenomena that are observed with preeminence in every respect are entirely established within the pure wisdom of the dharmadhātu.
One should know that all such phenomena are, according to their measure, correct speech in correspondence with the bodhicitta, and follow great compassion toward all sentient beings.

This is the supreme dharma-gate of the equality of all phenomena, having a single object of focus and being associated with signlessness; because it comprehensively subsumes all dharmas such as the pāramitās, it corresponds in measure to whatever one practices.
Because they are associated with this, it is called the selflessness of all phenomena.
The wise should know that the teachings spoken by the Buddha arise in accordance with reality from the gates of liberation.
The wisdom of all Buddhas is unsurpassed, and the causal nature they teach is likewise boundless;
knowing that boundlessness as it truly is, they manifest it in accordance with all things.
The various gates of correspondence reveal all natures; They arise through skillful means as appropriate to the occasion.
The great wisdom that accomplishes all is fully perfected; I proclaim it for the sake of benefit and happiness.
Treatise on the Characteristics of the Mahāyāna, Scroll II, Part B.
